items.title: Anthropic names Harvard experimental physicist Christopher Stubbs to the Long-Term Benefit Trust — the trustee seat that elects a majority of its board, pre-IPO
items.summary: Anthropic announced on October 21, 2026 that it has appointed Christopher Stubbs, an experimental physicist and former Dean of Science at Harvard University, to its Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT). The LTBT is the governance body that elects a majority of Anthropic's board of directors through a special class of shares called Class T stock, and that currently has the authority to elect three board members. The trust's remit is to advise leadership on major decisions involving AI risks and societal impacts. Stubbs fills one of two previously open seats, leaving one still vacant. Harvard's Crimson reports that he joined less than three weeks after stepping down as the Faculty of Arts and Sciences' senior adviser on generative AI, a role in which he helped secure access to leading AI models — including Anthropic's Claude — for FAS affiliates. He remains an active Harvard faculty member and will continue to serve on the FAS' committee on generative AI. Trustees hold no equity and are paid on a time-based basis for their advisory work. Daniela Amodei cited Stubbs's track record of following data and evidence as the reason for the appointment. Fortune notes that the LTBT is an unusual corporate governance arrangement that will come under increased pressure if the company goes public, which it is widely expected to do as soon as November (same Bloomberg-sourced timeline the Public Benefit Fund item in today's am file references). Primary source: Anthropic news post. Secondary coverage: Fortune (Oct 21), The Harvard Crimson (Oct 22), Reuters-via-regional-radio, CryptoBriefing, Biztoc.
items.why_it_matters: This is the second governance-tooling move Anthropic has made in a week — this one is the LTBT (which handles board appointments), the one from the am file is the Public Benefit Fund (which earmarks equity for public purposes) — and together they are the clearest preview yet of the two-track governance structure Anthropic is planning to carry into a publicly-traded company. The LTBT is the more consequential of the two for how Anthropic actually gets run: it elects a majority of the board, so whoever sits on it has, over time, final say on who steers the company. A Harvard experimental physicist — not an AI researcher, not a lawyer, not a VC — is a specific choice that says something about how Anthropic wants the trust to think: Stubbs's background is in physics (dark energy, observational cosmology) and in running a large science faculty (he was Dean of Science at Harvard), which is a decision-under-uncertainty-and-institutional-constraint skill set rather than a technical-AI-expertise one. His recent role as FAS senior adviser on generative AI, where he spent his time negotiating institutional model access on behalf of Harvard faculty, means he has watched the Anthropic-customer relationship from the other side of the table for the past year — that is a specific kind of experience the trust didn't have before. The remaining open seat is the piece to watch: with one seat still vacant and the IPO reportedly weeks away, the trust's composition when Anthropic prices its shares is going to be the thing that governance-focused readers of the eventual S-1 look at first. The honest caveats: (1) the trust's actual exercise of its board-election power has been minimal to date — appointments have mostly tracked founder preference, so the test of whether the LTBT is a meaningful check comes when and if its interests diverge from management's; (2) the Class T stock structure is unusual enough that it is a plausible target for post-IPO shareholder litigation under Delaware law, and no public company has yet tested a comparable structure at scale; (3) "advises leadership on AI risks and societal impacts" is deliberately broad language that gives the trust room to move but doesn't commit it to anything specific. For Gabe, the direct practical read is thin, but the governance-structure signal is useful alongside the Public Benefit Fund item from this morning: Anthropic is building two separate structures (one for governance, one for equity dedication) to try to carry mission-driven commitments across the public-markets transition, and the Stubbs appointment is the first concrete personnel decision inside that structure. The piece worth tracking from here: who fills the second open LTBT seat, and whether that choice tilts the trust toward governance expertise (lawyers, former regulators) or toward technical / scientific judgment of the Stubbs type.

items.title: Anthropic opens 8–12 week guest investigator program for life sciences — academic/nonprofit/government PIs collaborate directly with Anthropic researchers, Claude access at no cost, outputs published and open-sourced
items.summary: Anthropic announced on October 22, 2026 that it is accepting applications for a guest investigator program in the life sciences. Selected principal investigators and their research groups collaborate directly with Anthropic researchers for 8–12 weeks on special projects — producing analyses, artifacts, and tools using Claude — with Anthropic running its models and harnesses at no cost to the investigators. Eligible applicants are principal investigators at academic institutions, nonprofits, or government labs; for-profit industry research groups are explicitly out of scope. The program is focused on five domains: causal human biology, structural and computational molecular biology, medicinal chemistry, drug discovery, and clinical science. Investigators retain full data rights throughout and over any independent follow-on research; Anthropic does not ask for data access, and applications are explicitly instructed to include only publicly available information. Outputs are expected to be published, with accompanying data and code open-sourced. The application window is open for about 14 days, with selected applicants notified by email about 14 days after the window closes. The post positions the program alongside two existing Anthropic life-sciences efforts: the Life Sciences Verification Program (which gives qualified scientists access to Anthropic's most capable publicly available models for biology work) and the AI for Science initiative (which provides Claude credits to researchers). Primary source: anthropic.com/news post, directly WebFetch-verified.
items.why_it_matters: This is a specific kind of lab-academic collaboration structure worth looking at, because it is doing something the standard "here are free credits" model doesn't: it puts Anthropic researchers inside the collaboration for a bounded 8–12 week window, with the explicit expectation that the output is a publishable artifact with open-sourced data and code. That is closer to a traditional residency or sabbatical structure than it is to a developer-grant program. The published-and-open-sourced requirement is the part that matters structurally: it means Anthropic can't use the program to accumulate proprietary private datasets from the research, and it means the artifacts produced are available to the broader research community rather than becoming a Claude-only resource. The five domain areas (causal human biology, structural/computational molecular biology, medicinal chemistry, drug discovery, clinical science) are the same areas where Anthropic has been building out its biosecurity and life-sciences capacity for the past year — the UK AI Biosecurity Lab item in today's am file is the sovereign-defense version of the same thing — so this is the civilian-science complement to those partnerships, aimed at the labs that do foundational biology work rather than at government-funded threat detection. The exclusion of for-profit industry labs is a signal about what Anthropic is trying to buy with the program: not revenue, not customer validation, but credibility inside the academic biology community, and a pipeline of researchers who have shipped something useful with Claude. For Gabe, the direct practical relevance is low (the program is for principal investigators at biology labs), but the structural point is useful as context for how frontier labs are now partnering with science outside their own walls: not by selling API access, but by embedding researchers for a season on a specific project, with the deliverable being a public paper and open code. The honest caveats: (1) 8–12 weeks is tight for a wet-lab biology project — the useful fit is probably computational, analytical, or theoretical work, not experimental; (2) "special projects" is deliberately vague about what Anthropic will and won't take on, so the program's actual scope will depend on what the first cohort looks like; (3) Anthropic naming Claude by model class (Opus, standard models) in the related programs but not in this one leaves open the question of which models — including whether this includes early access to Mythos-class or similar restricted-access models — will actually be available to guest investigators. The piece to watch from here: whether the first cohort's published outputs are novel-biology or mostly workflow/benchmarking artifacts, which will tell you whether Anthropic is actually equipped to do co-authored biology work or whether the program is better understood as a sophisticated form of model-feedback collection.
